title: DynamoDB Cost: Capacity Modes, Table Classes & TTL
summary: On-demand vs provisioned capacity, reserved capacity, Standard-IA tables and TTL deletes.
tldr: **Capacity mode follows traffic shape.** New, unknown or spiky traffic → **on-demand** (pay per request, no throttling from under-provisioning). Steady, predictable traffic → **provisioned with auto scaling**, plus **reserved capacity** for the baseline.
**Table class follows the cost split.** When storage dominates and items are read rarely, switch to **Standard-IA**: much cheaper storage, slightly higher request prices, same API and latency.
**TTL** deletes expired items in the background at no write cost, which replaces scan-and-delete jobs.

keyFacts.text: Standard-IA table class cuts storage price versus Standard, with higher read/write prices. Best when storage is the main cost. Changing the class needs no code change.
Items whose TTL timestamp has passed are removed in the background without consuming write capacity, typically within a few days of expiry.
Reserved capacity (1 or 3 years) applies only to provisioned capacity on the Standard table class, not to on-demand or Standard-IA tables.
On-demand bills each read and write request, so near-idle tables cost almost nothing and sudden spikes need no capacity planning.

comparisons.title: Compare: DynamoDB cost choices
rows: Higher unit price for sustained high throughput
New app, no traffic history, campaign spikes
Traffic has been flat and predictable for a year
Storage is most of the bill

keywords.cue: no traffic history, jumps from near zero to tens of thousands of requests
steady, predictable high throughput 24 hours a day on on-demand
keywords.answer: Provisioned with auto scaling plus reserved capacity

keywords.cue: storage is 70–85% of the DynamoDB bill, data read rarely
single-digit millisecond lookups on old data, least app change
keywords.answer: Standard-IA table class (same API and latency)

keywords.cue: scheduled job scans and deletes expired items
remove session records 24 hours after creation
keywords.answer: TTL attribute set to creation time plus 24 hours

traps: DAX speeds up reads and can cut read capacity, but it adds node cost and does nothing for write or storage cost.
Global tables add replicas and replicated writes, which increase cost; they are for multi-Region access, not savings.
Switching to on-demand doesn't make scan-and-delete jobs cheaper; TTL removes the work entirely.
Exporting old items to S3 and querying with Athena breaks single-digit-millisecond lookups through the existing app.
Provisioned capacity sized for peak wastes money between spikes; use on-demand or auto scaling instead.
